name: ATAN
description: ATAN returns the arctangent, or inverse tangent, of a number. The result is the angle in radians whose tangent is the given number, ranging from -π/2 to π/2.
tldr: Returns the angle (in radians) whose tangent is the supplied number.

parameters.name: number
parameters.description: The tangent of the angle you want; any real number is accepted.

basicExample.description: Find the angle whose tangent is 1
basicExample.explanation: The arctangent of 1 is π/4 radians (45°).

advancedExamples.title: Convert the result to degrees
advancedExamples.explanation: ATAN(1) is π/4 radians, which DEGREES converts to 45°.

advancedExamples.title: Use when you only know the slope
advancedExamples.scenario: A line has slope 0.5; find its angle.
advancedExamples.explanation: ATAN(0.5) gives the angle whose tangent is 0.5, about 26.57°.

howItWorks: ATAN is the inverse of TAN. For any real x it returns the unique angle θ in (-π/2, π/2) (radians) such that tan(θ) = x. It cannot distinguish opposite quadrants, so use ATAN2 when both coordinates are known.

howToSteps.name: Pick the cell
howToSteps.text: Select the cell for the result.

howToSteps.name: Press Enter
howToSteps.text: The angle in radians appears; wrap with DEGREES if needed.

limitations: The result is in radians, not degrees.
ATAN uses only one argument, so it cannot tell which of two opposite quadrants the angle is in; ATAN2 resolves this with two coordinates.
Result range is limited to -π/2 to π/2.

commonErrors.fix: Supply a numeric value or a numeric cell reference.

googleSheetsEquivalent.description: ATAN works identically in Google Sheets.

faq.question: ATAN or ATAN2 — which should I use?
faq.answer: Use ATAN when you only have a single ratio (y/x). Use ATAN2 when you have separate x and y coordinates, because it places the angle in the correct quadrant.

faq.question: Why does ATAN(-1) give a negative angle?
faq.answer: ATAN's range is -π/2 to π/2, so negative inputs yield negative angles.

faq.question: Does ATAN return degrees?
faq.answer: No, it returns radians; use DEGREES or multiply by 180/PI().
